title: Punnett squares
examples: What does it mean if a trait is dominant?
How do I use the Punnett square to predict offspring?
Is the genotype always the same as the phenotype?

explain.say: Today we are learning about predicting traits in plants and animals. We will use a tool called a Punnett square. This helps us see possible combinations of genes.
Some genes are dominant, meaning they show up even if only one copy is present. Other genes are recessive, and they only show up if two copies are present.
The genotype is the actual combination of genes an organism carries. For example, we might write it as AA or Aa.
The phenotype is what the organism actually looks like. It is the physical trait we can see, like flower color. A genotype can lead to one phenotype.
Probability helps us guess the chances of certain traits in offspring. We use ratios to show these chances, like one quarter chance.
In real life, if a parent has brown eyes and a parent has blue eyes, the child might have brown eyes. This shows how genes combine.

faq.q: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
faq.a: The genotype is the letters representing the genes, like Aa. The phenotype is the actual physical trait you can see, like purple flowers.
asks: What is the difference between genes and traits?
Can I see the genotype if I only look at the phenotype?

faq.q: Does the dominant gene always mask the recessive gene?
faq.a: Yes, generally, the dominant allele will express its trait even if a recessive allele is also present. However, sometimes interactions are more complex.
asks: If I have two different genes, which one wins?
What happens when a dominant and recessive gene are together?

faq.q: How do I calculate the probability from a Punnett square?
faq.a: You count the possible outcomes in the boxes and then count how many match the trait you want. You divide that number by the total number of boxes.
asks: Is the probability always a percentage?
If I get one result, does that change the probability for the next one?

faq.q: Do I need to use capital letters for dominant genes?
faq.a: Yes, it is standard practice to use a capital letter for the dominant allele and a lowercase letter for the recessive allele. This helps keep track.
asks: What do the letters stand for?
Should I use symbols or letters for genes?

faq.q: Can I predict traits for more than two parents?
faq.a: Punnett squares are best for predicting traits from two parents. For more, you would need to use more complex probability rules.
asks: Does this work for three parents?
Is there a square for three parents?

facts: Dominant traits are always visible if present.
Recessive traits need two copies of the gene to show up.
The genotype is the gene code, while the phenotype is the physical trait.
Probability tells us the chance, not a guarantee, of an outcome.

quiz.say: A plant with the genotype BB will have which phenotype?
quiz.why: Since B is dominant for purple flowers, having two B genes means the trait will definitely show up.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the dominant gene B always overrides the recessive gene for white flowers.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the phenotype is what you see, not the letters you write down.
wrong.3: This is wrong because every organism has a visible physical trait based on its genes.

quiz.say: If an organism has the genotype Bb, what is its phenotype?
quiz.why: Because B is dominant, the presence of even one B gene makes the flower purple, even with the recessive b gene present.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the dominant allele B masks the recessive trait.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the phenotype describes the appearance, not the letter combination.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the trait is usually expressed fully by the dominant gene.
